title: SyMerge: From Non-Interference to Synergistic Merging via Single-Layer Adaptation
topic: General Machine Learning->Transfer, Multitask and Meta-learning
claim: Methods that avoid adaptation degrade sharply under distribution shift, while our adaptive method stays robust and best under corruption.
layout: single grouped bar chart, left-to-right, shaded test-time region, red box on ours
description: A single grouped bar chart of accuracy (%) with the y-axis from 50 to 100. Each method on the x-axis has a blue bar for original (clean) accuracy and a yellow bar for accuracy under corruption. The methods are TA, PCB, Consen, LiNeS, Iso-CTS, Ada, Surgery, WEMoE and Ours. The right four methods sit on a gray shaded background labeled 'Test-time adaptation'. Training-free methods on the left have clean accuracy of about 80–89% and corruption accuracy of about 56–65%. The test-time methods reach about 89–93% clean and about 67–69% under corruption. 'Ours' is in bold, and its yellow corruption bar has a thick red outline at about 74%, which is clearly the highest. A legend in the upper left explains the colors. The eye goes first to the red-boxed bar, then to the large blue-yellow gaps on the left.
caption: Training-Free methods collapse under corruption. Worse than test-time methods on clean data as well, and far more degraded under corruption.
abstract: Model merging combines independently trained models into a single multi-task model. However, most existing approaches focus primarily on avoiding task interference. We argue that its greater potential lies in enabling task synergy, where tasks actively improve one another. We identify cross-task performance, defined by compatibility between encoders and predictors across tasks, as a key indicator of merge quality. We demonstrate that adapting only a single task-specific layer is sufficient to induce such synergy. This study proposes SyMerge, a lightweight framework that jointly optimizes merging coefficients and a single task-specific layer. We adopt an expert-guided self-labeling objective, providing stable supervision beyond entropy minimization. Intriguingly, we further show that SyMerge successfully merges models trained from different initializations, a regime where standard methods break down. Our minimalist yet principled method achieves state-of-the-art results across vision, dense prediction, and NLP benchmarks. Our code is available at https://aim-skku.github.io/SyMerge
